The daguangxian is a Chinese bowed string instrument of the huqin family, made up of a soundbox, a neck, tuning pegs, strings and a bow. The traditional soundbox is made from the trunk of the pandanus or the agave, the soundboard is mostly Taiwan paulownia, and the neck and pegs are of bamboo or wood; it carries two strings tuned a perfect fifth apart. To play, the instrument is held upright with the soundbox on the left thigh, the bow is drawn across the strings, and traditionally the strings are stopped with the pads of the fingers. It is current in Taiwan, southern Fujian and the Chaoshan region, where Hakka and Minnan communities use it in gezi storytelling, gezi opera, beiguan, zhengyin opera, baizi opera, street formations and Lingbao Daoist ritual accompaniment.
大廣弦為兩弦弦鳴樂器，演奏時將琴身直立，琴筒置於左大腿上，以弓擦弦發聲。琴上張兩: The daguangxian is a two-string chordophone; it is held upright with the soundbox on the left thigh and sounds as the bow is drawn across the strings. The two strings are tuned a perfect fifth apart; traditionally the strings are stopped with the pads of the fingers, the fingertips turned inward. A beginner can work in this order: first steady the position of the instrument, then bring the bow into contact with the strings, change the pitch by stopping the strings, and practise basic bowing in accompaniment settings such as gezi storytelling and gezi opera.

The source calls it a lower-pitched mezzo instrument whose characteristic sound is a 'wailing'; it is often used to accompany gezi storytelling and gezi opera, and it leads the jianghu tune, the kudiao ('weeping tune') and the zanian tune. Compared with the Chaoshan bamboo fiddle, which is made entirely of bamboo and has a higher, more excited timbre close to the touxian or the jinghu, the daguangxian lies lower. 大廣弦為胡琴類兩弦拉弦樂器，主要流行於台灣、閩南與潮汕，用於歌仔說唱、歌仔戲、北: The daguangxian is a two-string bowed instrument of the huqin kind, mainly current in Taiwan, southern Fujian and Chaoshan, used in gezi storytelling, gezi opera, beiguan, zhengyin opera and baizi opera, and it was also used in the stage band of early Chaozhou opera. In gezi opera it is the second string, and together with the kezixian, yueqin and pinzi it makes up the 'four great pieces'; Wang Siming, Wen Hongtu and Chen Yu'an all made recordings, and Wen Hongtu's pupil Lu Peisen was the last daguangxian storytelling performer in Xiamen. In Chaoshan it now mostly survives in written records, and the Chaozhou opera band no longer uses it. From the second half of the twentieth century it entered newly composed folk music, such as Xiangyin Jihuai, Yuanxiang yu Bentu and the 'Taiwan Scenes Suite: Temple Fair'.

The neck and pegs are of bamboo or wood. It carries two strings: silk strings were common early on, steel is now usual, and some have a steel outer string and a silk inner string, or use double strings, or one string of artificial fibre.
